annotations.keyFindings: Twelve apps assigned the correct urgency level for 49 percent of 200 vignettes (33 to 71 percent by app); emergency vignettes were correctly escalated in 78 percent; 41 percent of self-care vignettes were over-triaged.
App and nurse agreed for 61 percent of 1,210 real callers; the app advised lower urgency for 11 percent, including 3 of 46 callers sent to an emergency department; agreement 52 percent over age 70.
annotations.limitations: Nurse not blinded in the first month; one advice line.

annotations.keyFindings: Apps identified emergencies in 64 percent of paediatric vignettes; fever in infants under three months was under-triaged by five of eight apps.
Accuracy fell by 12 percentage points when vignettes were worded as lay users describe symptoms.
annotations.notes: Explains why vignette accuracy overstates real-world accuracy.

annotations.keyFindings: Accuracy changed by up to 14 points between versions of the same app over 18 months, in both directions.
Patients with limited English or low health literacy abandoned the app more often (29 against 9 percent) and more often received lower-urgency advice.

claims.text: Across twelve apps tested with clinician-written vignettes, the correct urgency level was assigned in about half of cases, and emergencies were correctly escalated in 78 percent.
claims.passage: Apps assigned the correct urgency level in 49 percent of vignettes on average, ranging from 33 to 71 percent between apps.
claims.interpretation: Vignette accuracy is moderate at best and varies widely between apps.

claims.text: With real callers, an app advised lower urgency than a triage nurse for 11 percent of callers, including 3 of 46 callers the nurse sent to an emergency department.
claims.passage: The app advised a lower urgency than the nurse for 11 percent of callers, including 3 of the 46 callers whom the nurse sent to an emergency department.
claims.interpretation: Under-triage of emergencies occurs with real users.

claims.text: Accuracy was 12 percentage points lower when vignettes used the words lay users choose.
claims.passage: Accuracy for the correct urgency level was 12 percentage points lower with lay-worded vignettes.
claims.interpretation: Clinician-written vignette studies overstate real-world accuracy.

claims.text: Accuracy of the same app varied by up to 14 percentage points between versions over 18 months.
claims.passage: Accuracy for the correct urgency level varied by up to 14 percentage points between versions of the same app.
claims.interpretation: Any endorsement should be tied to a version and re-tested.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Vignette studies show apps assigning the correct urgency level in about half of cases, with wide variation between apps, frequent over-triage and poorer performance for infants with fever. Lay wording lowers accuracy further, and accuracy drifts between versions. The only real-patient comparison found under-triage of some emergencies and lower agreement for older callers, and people with limited English or low health literacy were served worse. No study supports a claim that apps identify emergencies almost always.
gradeRationale: Mostly vignette studies with indirectness to real use, one real-patient comparison with partial blinding, small single-site equity data; consistent concerns, low certainty.
summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four claims recorded; overall certainty low.
